title: All-on-X vs Dentures: A Complete Guide for Valencia Patients

body:
If your dentist has recommended replacing a full arch of teeth, you are probably weighing All-on-X against dentures right now. The choice affects how you chew, how much daily maintenance you take on and, often, your budget. This guide compares the two on cost, stability, bone health, recovery and long-term care, and lists the questions to bring to your consultation with Dr. Nuriel Lavi at Valencia Dentistry in Santa Clarita. For the fixed option itself, see our [All-on-4 implants](/services/oral-surgery/all-on-4-implants/) service page.

## Why this decision matters

Full-arch fixed implants such as All-on-X are designed to feel like permanent teeth. Traditional dentures remain a removable, lower-cost option. Which is better for you depends on your bone, medical history, budget and how you use your mouth. If you are new to the practice, our [first-visit guide](/why-choose-valencia-smile-what-to-expect-on-your-first-visit/) explains what imaging and paperwork to bring.

## Quick side-by-side comparison

The table below summarizes the typical trade-offs. The numbers are typical U.S. ranges drawn from clinical reviews, not Valencia Dentistry pricing; see the cost section below for context.

| Feature | All-on-X (full-arch implants) | Traditional dentures |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Typical upfront cost (per arch) | $15,000 to $50,000 (All-on-4 commonly $15,000 to $30,000) | $600 to $8,000 (basic to premium) |
| Stability and chewing | High; fixed to implants, with chewing force close to natural teeth | Variable; removable, with considerably lower chewing force |
| Bone preservation | Yes; implants transmit force into bone and slow resorption | No; a denture resting on the ridge does not prevent shrinkage |
| Maintenance | Daily care plus routine professional checks; occasional prosthesis maintenance | Daily soaking and cleaning, relines every few years, adhesives often needed |
| Typical lifespan | Implant fixtures can last decades; prosthesis may be renewed after 10 to 20 years | 5 to 10 years for fit; relines and replacement are common |

## Real costs and what changes the price

Expect wide variation based on location, implant system, whether bone grafting or sinus lifts are needed, and the prosthetic material. Nationally, full-arch fixed solutions commonly fall between $15,000 and $50,000 per arch, while well-made dentures typically range from a few hundred dollars to under $10,000 for premium lab work. For a local pricing walkthrough and an itemized checklist to bring to consultations, see our [Valencia implant cost guide](/dental-implants-valencia-cost-guide/).

Clinical literature most commonly reports implant survival between 90 and 98 percent over 10 years for properly placed implants, depending on risk factors and prosthesis type; see the systematic review at [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4647895/). Dentures do not have a survival statistic in the same sense because they need relines, rebasing or replacement as the jaw changes.

## What patients commonly report

Patient discussions online tend to repeat three themes, and they match what we hear in the office:

- **Adhesives and fit.** Denture wearers often describe messy adhesives and repeated relines, especially with lower dentures.
- **Immediate-load expectations.** Same-day All-on-4 workflows surprise people, in a good way, but they raise practical questions about healing and about smoking or vaping, both of which affect healing and success.
- **Pain, infection and follow-up.** Surgical pain, recovery length and infection are common concerns, and the consistent advice is to choose an experienced provider and be honest about medical risks such as uncontrolled diabetes or smoking.

## Who is a good candidate for each option

Both options are valid. Match the decision to the outcome you need:

- **All-on-X is most appropriate if** you want fixed teeth, have enough bone or are willing to graft, want stronger chewing, and can plan for a higher upfront cost with less frequent replacement.
- **Traditional dentures are reasonable if** you cannot have surgery, need the lowest upfront cost, want a non-surgical immediate solution, or have medical risks such as uncontrolled conditions or heavy smoking that make implants a poor fit.

For older adults with health concerns, see [dental implants for seniors](/dental-implants-for-seniors-safety-success/). Age alone is not a reason to rule out implants; health control and bone quantity drive the decision.

## What to expect if you choose All-on-X

Workflows vary by practice. A typical plan follows these steps:

1. Consultation with 3D CBCT imaging and digital study models
2. Medical clearance and, if needed, preparatory extractions or grafting
3. Surgical placement (All-on-4 often uses four angled implants per arch)
4. An immediate provisional fixed bridge in many same-day protocols, or delayed loading if bone quality needs healing time
5. Follow-up visits for hygiene, bite adjustments and the final prosthesis once the implants integrate

Patients who have same-day All-on-4 often value not being without teeth, but realistic recovery expectations matter. Our [All-on-X recovery timeline](/all-on-x-recovery-timeline/) covers that in detail. On smoking: it increases the chance of implant complications, and most clinicians recommend stopping during healing and ideally quitting.

## Clinical risks and uncomfortable truths

Implants are highly successful when placed well by a coordinated team. Still, be aware of these caveats:

- **Peri-implantitis and maintenance.** Implants need lifelong care; infection around an implant is a real risk and can be costly to treat.
- **Hidden costs.** Surgical staging, grafting and prosthetic upgrades can raise the final price. Ask for an itemized estimate and a contingency budget.
- **Not everyone gets ideal immediate results.** Same-day provisionals sometimes need extensive adjustment, and healing can be slower with smoking or poor metabolic control.

## Cost comparison with a lifetime view

| Treatment | Typical upfront cost (U.S.) | Maintenance and lifetime notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| All-on-4 or All-on-X (fixed, per arch) | $15,000 to $30,000 typical; premium labs or zirconia bridges can push toward $40,000 or more | Maintenance visits, night guards, screw re-torques; prosthesis renewal possible every 10 to 20 years |
| Implant-retained overdenture (2 to 4 implants) | $7,000 to $25,000 per arch | Better stability than conventional dentures; attachments need periodic replacement |
| Traditional complete denture (both arches) | $600 to $8,000 | Relines and replacements commonly every 5 to 10 years; progressive jaw resorption affects fit and appearance |

## Consultation checklist

Bring these items and ask for them explicitly:

- CBCT or 3D imaging, not just a panoramic X-ray; this determines bone quantity for implants
- A written, itemized estimate: surgeon fee, implant parts, lab, provisional, final prosthesis and any grafts
- A clear timeline from provisional to final bridge, and the number of follow-ups
- Before-and-after photos of similar full-arch cases from this practice
- How the team manages complications such as peri-implantitis, and what happens if an implant fails
- Anesthesia and sedation options, and the expected recovery for your health profile

## How we counsel patients who are undecided

Dr. Lavi starts with function: can you eat what you want now? If not, and you want a fixed, long-term solution, implants often make sense. If you want the lowest upfront cost and a non-surgical path, dentures remain a sound choice. Either way, get imaging, request an itemized plan, ask about contingency plans and check the long-term follow-up protocol.

## Making the decision

Choosing between All-on-X and dentures comes down to function, long-term value and your health. All-on-X offers greater stability, preserves bone and restores far more natural chewing, but needs a higher upfront investment and surgical candidacy. Dentures are faster and cheaper up front but require ongoing maintenance and do not prevent ridge resorption. For an imaging-based consultation in Valencia, call (661) 254-5200 or book online, and bring the checklist above.

*References:* long-term implant outcome reviews at [NCBI](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC4647895/); denture overview at the [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/tests-procedures/denture/about/pac-20384885). For a broader comparison, see [dental implants vs dentures](/dental-implants-vs-dentures/).

faq.q: How much does All-on-X cost versus dentures?
faq.a: Up front, dentures are far cheaper: a full-arch denture typically ranges from $600 to $8,000, while full-arch implant solutions commonly run $15,000 to $50,000 per arch depending on materials, lab fees and grafting. Over a lifetime, dentures need relines and replacement more often, while implants slow bone loss and may prove more cost-effective.

faq.q: Will All-on-X stop bone loss where dentures do not?
faq.a: Implants stimulate the jaw and slow the bone resorption that leads to a sunken facial appearance. Conventional dentures rest on the ridge without stimulating bone, so the ridge shrinks over time and the fit deteriorates.

faq.q: Do All-on-X procedures hurt, and how long is recovery?
faq.a: Placement is done under local anesthesia, often with sedation. Expect swelling and discomfort for several days; most patients return to light activity within a week. Immediate-load provisionals mean you leave with teeth the same day, but the mouth still needs weeks to heal, so follow your post-operative instructions closely.

faq.q: Can I smoke after All-on-X or implant surgery?
faq.a: Smoking slows healing and increases the risk of implant failure. The usual clinical recommendation is to stop during healing and ideally quit for long-term implant health. Discuss realistic timelines for tobacco or vaping with your surgeon.

faq.q: What are the maintenance and long-term costs after All-on-X?
faq.a: Maintenance includes routine hygiene visits, occasional prosthesis adjustments and repairs. Implant fixtures can last decades, but the prosthetic bridge may need replacement after 10 to 20 years. Ask for an itemized long-term care plan.
